impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims for treating headache with an anti-CGRP antagonist antibody genus when identifying members of the genus requires undue experimentation, even though any member of the genus would satisfy the treatment limitation.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against Eli Lilly's enablement challenge. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines Amgen v. Sanofi enablement standards for method claims and sustains overly broad claims that will stifle medical innovation. The decision creates important precedent distinguishing enablement analysis for method claims from composition claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, potentially preserving valuable pharmaceutical patents covering antibody genera where any member of the genus is therapeutically effective.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors face broader patent blocking positions in the biopharmaceutical space, as the decision may sustain genus-level method claims that restrict development of alternative antibodies for the same therapeutic indication.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of proprietary automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the district court's override of the jury's breach of contract damages award, reinstating it. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and MUTSA. This case involves Ford's development of competing software (PDO) after licensing Versata's automotive configuration tools.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret holders benefit from broader acceptance of damages methodologies and protection against licensees who develop competing products using licensed technology. The reinstatement of the jury's contract damages award supports enforcement of software licensing agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that license software and later develop in-house alternatives face heightened trade secret misappropriation risk and potential damages exposure, particularly when the replacement product was developed during the licensing relationship.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive patent license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' sufficient for the licensee to sue in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to an enforcement-only business model triggered an automatic termination clause.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, making TexasLDPC the effective patent owner with standing to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to patent enforcement did not constitute cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the license agreement.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from confirmation that exclusive licenses conveying all substantial rights create standing to sue independently, and that pivoting to enforcement-focused business models does not necessarily terminate the license.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a defense based on challenging licensee standing, and licensors may find it harder to regain control over patent enforcement when exclusive licensees shift to assertion-only models.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems satisfy the subject matter eligibility requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents in a case involving digital communication technology used in televisions. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, preserving a jury verdict against LG. The split outcome provides guidance on how § 101 eligibility analysis applies to signal processing and communication technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the communications technology space benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain claim formulations and preservation of jury infringement and damages verdicts, providing guidance on drafting eligible claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry-standard communication protocols face continued patent infringement exposure, and the partial vacatur of eligibility creates uncertainty about the boundary between eligible and ineligible claims in this technology area.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination, or whether such dispute is a state law contract matter.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over a dispute about whether patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination for purposes of triggering a contingent payment under a settlement agreement. The court determined the dispute was fundamentally a state law contract interpretation issue that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question, and transferred the case to the Fifth Circuit.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties drafting patent settlement agreements receive clarity that disputes over contingent payment triggers tied to reexamination outcomes may be adjudicated in regional circuits applying state contract law rather than the Federal Circuit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies with patent settlement agreements containing reexamination-contingent payments face uncertainty about which court will resolve disputes, potentially leading to forum-shopping complications and inconsistent interpretations of patent-related contract terms.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a wireless communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for indefiniteness or lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the final judgment of invalidity, reversing the district court's indefiniteness ruling but finding the claims invalid for lack of enablement. The court held that while the claims were not indefinite, the patent's specification failed to enable the full scope of the claimed invention. This decision reinforces the enablement requirement as a meaningful constraint on claim scope in wireless communications patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from a strong affirmance that enablement requirements serve as an independent check on overly broad patent claims, even when definiteness is established.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with broad wireless communications claims face heightened enablement scrutiny, particularly where claims cover embodiments that the specification does not adequately teach.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly dismissed a patent infringement complaint without leave to amend, awarded attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and imposed sanctions on plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of VDPP's patent infringement complaint against Volkswagen without leave to amend, finding the proposed amended complaint was futile. The court also upheld the award of $207,543.60 in attorney fees to Volkswagen under § 285 and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel. The decision reinforces consequences for pursuing frivolous patent infringement claims, particularly where pre-suit damages allegations lack adequate factual support.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from robust fee-shifting and sanctions enforcement against weak patent assertions, deterring frivolous patent litigation and reducing defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent plaintiffs and their counsel face significant financial exposure through fee awards and personal sanctions when pursuing infringement claims that courts deem inadequately supported, raising the stakes for pre-suit investigation.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 and a related patent was invalidated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and attorney fees, finding the court's order lacked sufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved Epic Tech's pursuit of infringement claims on an electronic gaming patent despite multiple PTO rejections of related applications under § 101 and a related patent's invalidation. The decision signals heightened scrutiny of patent enforcement when the plaintiff had substantial notice of eligibility problems.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from stronger appellate review of fee and sanctions decisions, increasing the likelihood that exceptional case findings will be made when patent holders pursue claims despite significant prior § 101 rejections.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders pursuing enforcement of patents in art areas where related patents or applications have been rejected under § 101 face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions, requiring more careful pre-suit evaluation.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to oil and gas wellbore float tools, and whether the jury's infringement and validity findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment finding infringement and validity of claims in a patent relating to oil and gas casing float tools. The case involves disputed claim construction of the term 'internal diameter' that is critical to determining whether Nine Energy's competing BreakThru Casing Flotation Device infringes. The outcome will significantly affect competition in the oil and gas completion tools market.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the oil and gas equipment space benefit from closer appellate scrutiny of claim construction, potentially narrowing the scope of competitors' patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the energy services industry face uncertainty and additional litigation costs from vacated judgments, potentially delaying enforcement of patent rights against competing products.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate salt forms, pharmaceutical formulations, and methods of treatment satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that the asserted claims of three Exelixis patents covering crystalline forms of cabozantinib malate (the API in Cabometyx® for cancer treatment) have adequate written description. The decision protects Exelixis's patent portfolio covering its blockbuster cancer drug against generic entry by MSN Laboratories, reinforcing the strength of pharmaceutical polymorph and salt-form patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies benefit from confirmation that well-characterized crystalline polymorph patents satisfy written description requirements, strengthening barriers to generic competition and protecting substantial R&D investments in drug development.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical companies face continued patent barriers to market entry for important cancer treatments, as salt-form and polymorph patents remain enforceable even when the underlying active ingredient is known.

impacts.caseName: Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi ve Ticaret A.S. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce properly used the invoice date rather than an alternative date as the 'date of sale' for purposes of calculating antidumping duty rates on Turkish steel rebar imports under 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed Commerce's use of the invoice date as the date of sale for calculating antidumping duties on Turkish steel rebar imports. The decision upholds Commerce's regulatory presumption under § 351.401(i) that the invoice date normally reflects when material terms of sale are established. This ruling impacts the calculation of antidumping duty rates affecting the competitiveness of imported steel products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic steel producers and trade coalitions benefit from the affirmation of Commerce's standard methodology for calculating antidumping duties, maintaining trade protection against below-market imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign steel exporters face continued application of Commerce's invoice-date presumption, which may result in higher antidumping duty rates compared to alternative date-of-sale methodologies that could better reflect actual pricing negotiations.
